Exaltation of Christ
eg-zawl-TAY-shuhn uhv KRYST
doctrinal phrase
From exalt (Latin exaltare, to lift up high) and Christ; the doctrine of the stages by which the humbled Christ was raised to glory.

See also: Exaltation of Christ

📖 Biblical Definition

The exaltation of Christ is the doctrine of the stages by which the Lord Jesus, after His state of humiliation, was raised to glory and dominion. The Reformed catechisms reckon the exaltation in four steps: His resurrection from the dead on the third day, His ascension up into heaven, His sitting at the right hand of God the Father, and His coming again to judge the world at the last day. Having humbled Himself and become obedient unto death, even the death of the cross, He was for that obedience highly exalted, given a name above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow. The exaltation is the Father’s public vindication of the Son and His acceptance of the finished work of the cross: the One condemned by men is justified by God, raised, enthroned, and crowned. From His exalted session Christ reigns over all things for His church, pours out the Holy Spirit, intercedes for His people as their great High Priest, subdues His enemies, and gathers His elect. The exaltation is also the pattern and pledge of the believer’s hope, for the same Lord who was abased and then glorified will raise and glorify all who are united to Him. The dictionary holds the exaltation as the triumphant counterpart to the humiliation: the way down was the way up, and the crucified Servant is now the reigning Lord.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The doctrine of the four stages—resurrection, ascension, session at God’s right hand, and return in judgment—by which the humbled Christ was raised to glory and dominion.

EXALTATION OF CHRIST, the raising of the humbled Christ to glory.

Reckoned in four stages: resurrection, ascension, session, and return in judgment.

The Father’s vindication of the Son and acceptance of the finished work of the cross.

For His obedience unto death, He was given a name above every name.

The pattern and pledge of the believer’s own resurrection and glory.

📖 Key Scripture

Php 2:9 — "Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name:"

Act 2:33 — "Therefore being by the right hand of God exalted, and having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Ghost, he hath shed forth this, which ye now see and hear."

Act 5:31 — "Him hath God exalted with his right hand to be a Prince and a Saviour, for to give repentance to Israel, and forgiveness of sins."

Eph 1:20 — "Which he wrought in Christ, when he raised him from the dead, and set him at his own right hand in the heavenly places,"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The exaltation is reduced to a symbol of the cause’s survival, denying the bodily resurrection, ascension, and present reign of Christ.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the bodily and historical reality of each stage of the exaltation. Christ rose bodily, ascended visibly, sits enthroned at the Father’s right hand, and will return in person to judge. Against the liberal reduction that treats the resurrection as the survival of Jesus’ influence or the disciples’ rekindled faith, the dictionary holds that the same body that hung on the cross was raised, exalted, and glorified.

Where a corruption presses, it is the eclipse of Christ’s present reign. Many treat the ascension as a mere disappearance and forget that Christ is now actively reigning, interceding, and ruling all things for His church. The exalted Christ is not absent but enthroned; He governs history, subdues His enemies, and will not rest until every knee bows. The believer’s comfort is that his Saviour is not merely a memory but a living, reigning Lord, and that the way of humiliation followed by exaltation is the road his own life and death will travel in Christ.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

The doctrine traces the upward stages by which the abased Christ was lifted to the throne.

expand to see more

Greek huperupsoō — to exalt to the highest place; “God also hath highly exalted him.”

The four stages: resurrection, ascension, session, and return in glory.

Set in deliberate contrast to the stages of humiliation.

The “right hand of God” — the place of honor, power, and royal rule.

Philippians 2 binds the humiliation and exaltation in one great hymn to Christ.

Usage

"The exaltation of Christ is taught in four stages in the Reformed catechisms."

"It is preached as the Father’s vindication of the Son’s finished work."

"Christ’s present reign and intercession are stressed against treating the ascension as mere absence."
